claim: The nvTRPM2 protein shows ~63% sequence similarity (34% sequence identity) with human TRPM2 (hTRPM2).
source: The nvTRPM2 protein shows ~63% sequence similarity (34% sequence identity) with human TRPM2 (hTRPM2), and when expressed in mammalian cells, it forms functional channels opened by cytosolic ADPR (Kühn et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement about sequence comparison between nvTRPM2 and hTRPM2.

claim: When expressed in mammalian cells, nvTRPM2 forms functional channels opened by cytosolic ADPR.
source: The nvTRPM2 protein shows ~63% sequence similarity (34% sequence identity) with human TRPM2 (hTRPM2), and when expressed in mammalian cells, it forms functional channels opened by cytosolic ADPR (Kühn et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kühn et al., 2015.

claim: ADPR and intracellular Ca2+ act as obligate co-activators for nvTRPM2.
source: ADPR and intracellular Ca2+ acted as obligate co-activators, as addition of both ligands was required to open, whereas removal of either ligand was sufficient to close the channels (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating that both ligands are required for channel opening.

claim: Addition of both ADPR and Ca2+ is required to open nvTRPM2 channels.
source: ADPR and intracellular Ca2+ acted as obligate co-activators, as addition of both ligands was required to open, whereas removal of either ligand was sufficient to close the channels (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by experimental data in Figure 1A.

claim: Removal of either ADPR or Ca2+ is sufficient to close nvTRPM2 channels.
source: ADPR and intracellular Ca2+ acted as obligate co-activators, as addition of both ligands was required to open, whereas removal of either ligand was sufficient to close the channels (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by experimental data in Figure 1A.

claim: nvTRPM2 current elicited by saturating ADPR + Ca2+ was only modestly (by 10–20%) enhanced upon exposure to exogenous PIP2.
source: Although nvTRPM2 current elicited by saturating ADPR + Ca2+was only modestly (by 10–20%) enhanced upon exposure to exogenous PIP2 (Figure 1B, left blue bar), it was almost completely abolished when membrane PIP2 headgroups were masked with polylysine (Figure 1B, red bar), but could then be fully recovered by addition of exogenous PIP2 (Figure 1B, right blue bar).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: nvTRPM2 current was almost completely abolished when membrane PIP2 headgroups were masked with polylysine.
source: Although nvTRPM2 current elicited by saturating ADPR + Ca2+was only modestly (by 10–20%) enhanced upon exposure to exogenous PIP2 (Figure 1B, left blue bar), it was almost completely abolished when membrane PIP2 headgroups were masked with polylysine (Figure 1B, red bar), but could then be fully recovered by addition of exogenous PIP2 (Figure 1B, right blue bar).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: nvTRPM2 current could be fully recovered by addition of exogenous PIP2 after polylysine treatment.
source: Although nvTRPM2 current elicited by saturating ADPR + Ca2+was only modestly (by 10–20%) enhanced upon exposure to exogenous PIP2 (Figure 1B, left blue bar), it was almost completely abolished when membrane PIP2 headgroups were masked with polylysine (Figure 1B, red bar), but could then be fully recovered by addition of exogenous PIP2 (Figure 1B, right blue bar).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PIP2 is essential for nvTRPM2 activity.
source: Thus, PIP2 is also essential for nvTRPM2 activity, but is tightly bound, so that the channels remain close-to-saturated even at the low PIP2 concentration of an inside-out patch.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental observations with polylysine and exogenous PIP2.

claim: PIP2 is tightly bound to nvTRPM2, so that the channels remain close-to-saturated even at the low PIP2 concentration of an inside-out patch.
source: Thus, PIP2 is also essential for nvTRPM2 activity, but is tightly bound, so that the channels remain close-to-saturated even at the low PIP2 concentration of an inside-out patch.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that exogenous PIP2 only modestly enhances current.

claim: Gating regulation by ADPR, Ca2+, and PIP2 of nvTRPM2 is very similar to that of hTRPM2.
source: All in all, gating regulation by ADPR, Ca2+, and PIP2 of nvTRPM2 is very similar to that of hTRPM2 (Tóth and Csanády, 2012).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citation to Tóth and Csanády, 2012.

claim: The nvTRPM2 structure was refined to 3.1 Å resolution.
source: The final reconstruction, calculated with 72% of the particles from 3D classification, was refined to 3.1 Å resolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the resolution of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The final reconstruction was calculated with 72% of the particles from 3D classification.
source: The final reconstruction, calculated with 72% of the particles from 3D classification, was refined to 3.1 Å resolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data processing for the structure.

claim: The nvTRPM2 map showed excellent side chain densities in most of the regions.
source: This map showed excellent side chain densities in most of the regions, which allowed us to build ~1200 residues de novo without ambiguity.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the quality of the cryo-EM map.

claim: ~1200 residues were built de novo without ambiguity in the nvTRPM2 structure.
source: This map showed excellent side chain densities in most of the regions, which allowed us to build ~1200 residues de novo without ambiguity.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model building process.

claim: The C-terminal NUDT9H domain is entirely invisible in the density map.
source: The C-terminal NUDT9H domain, however, is entirely invisible in the density map, indicating that in the absence of ADPR this domain is flexibly linked to the core structure.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM map.

claim: In the absence of ADPR, the NUDT9H domain is flexibly linked to the core structure.
source: The C-terminal NUDT9H domain, however, is entirely invisible in the density map, indicating that in the absence of ADPR this domain is flexibly linked to the core structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of density for the NUDT9H domain in the map.

claim: The nvTRPM2 structure is shaped like a square prism with dimensions of 135 x 100 x 100 Å.
source: The nvTRPM2 structure is shaped like a square prism with dimensions of 135 x 100 x 100 Å (Figure 2A–C, color coded by subunits), and >80% of its volume is cytosolic.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the structure.

claim: >80% of the nvTRPM2 volume is cytosolic.
source: The nvTRPM2 structure is shaped like a square prism with dimensions of 135 x 100 x 100 Å (Figure 2A–C, color coded by subunits), and >80% of its volume is cytosolic.
evidence: This is a direct calculation from the structure.

claim: The overall architecture of nvTRPM2 resembles that of TRPM4 and TRPM8.
source: Consistent with the high sequence conservation within the TRPM subfamily (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), the overall architecture of nvTRPM2 (Figure 2D–E) resembles that of TRPM4 and TRPM8.
evidence: This is a structural comparison supported by visual inspection of the structures.

claim: In TRPM4, a high-affinity nucleotide binding site for inhibitory ATP, ADP, and AMP is located at the interface between the NTD and the ARD of the neighboring subunit.
source: For example, in TRPM4, a high-affinity nucleotide binding site for inhibitory ATP, ADP, and AMP is located at the interface between the NTD and the ARD of the neighboring subunit (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2017.

claim: In nvTRPM2, the nucleotide binding surface is differently arranged compared to TRPM4 and lacks residues important for nucleotide binding.
source: In nvTRPM2 the five long intertwined loops that build this surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 5, NTD, right surface and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, inset 3) are differently arranged, contain an extra β strand (β7b, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, inset 3), and lack residues important for nucleotide binding, explaining insensitivity of TRPM2 to these nucleotides.
evidence: This is a structural observation that explains functional differences.

claim: The different arrangement of the nucleotide binding surface in nvTRPM2 explains insensitivity of TRPM2 to ATP, ADP, and AMP.
source: In nvTRPM2 the five long intertwined loops that build this surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 5, NTD, right surface and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, inset 3) are differently arranged, contain an extra β strand (β7b, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, inset 3), and lack residues important for nucleotide binding, explaining insensitivity of TRPM2 to these nucleotides.
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural differences to functional properties.

claim: The selectivity filter of nvTRPM2 is short and wide.
source: The selectivity filter is short and wide (Figure 3A), the diameter at its narrowest point is ~5.2 Å (Figure 3B), larger than that of TRPM4 (~4.2 Å).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the structure.

claim: The diameter of the nvTRPM2 selectivity filter at its narrowest point is ~5.2 Å.
source: The selectivity filter is short and wide (Figure 3A), the diameter at its narrowest point is ~5.2 Å (Figure 3B), larger than that of TRPM4 (~4.2 Å).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the structure.

claim: The diameter of the TRPM4 selectivity filter at its narrowest point is ~4.2 Å.
source: The selectivity filter is short and wide (Figure 3A), the diameter at its narrowest point is ~5.2 Å (Figure 3B), larger than that of TRPM4 (~4.2 Å).
evidence: This is a measurement from TRPM4 structure used for comparison.

claim: The large diameter of the nvTRPM2 filter is consistent with functional properties of the hTRPM2 pore which permeates tetramethyl-ammonium (~5.8 Å) but not N-methyl-D-glucosamine (~6.8 Å).
source: Such a large diameter is consistent with functional properties of the hTRPM2 pore which permeates tetramethyl-ammonium (~5.8 Å) but not N-methyl-D-glucosamine (~6.8 Å) (Tóth and Csanády, 2012), and suggests that the TRPM2 filter allows hydrated ions to pass.
evidence: This connects structural measurements to functional data from Tóth and Csanády, 2012.

claim: The hTRPM2 pore permeates tetramethyl-ammonium (~5.8 Å) but not N-methyl-D-glucosamine (~6.8 Å).
source: Such a large diameter is consistent with functional properties of the hTRPM2 pore which permeates tetramethyl-ammonium (~5.8 Å) but not N-methyl-D-glucosamine (~6.8 Å) (Tóth and Csanády, 2012), and suggests that the TRPM2 filter allows hydrated ions to pass.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tóth and Csanády, 2012.

claim: The TRPM2 filter allows hydrated ions to pass.
source: Such a large diameter is consistent with functional properties of the hTRPM2 pore which permeates tetramethyl-ammonium (~5.8 Å) but not N-methyl-D-glucosamine (~6.8 Å) (Tóth and Csanády, 2012), and suggests that the TRPM2 filter allows hydrated ions to pass.
evidence: This is inferred from the large pore diameter and permeation properties.

claim: The nvTRPM2 filter is lined by the backbone atoms of Y1035 and G1036, and the side chain of E1037.
source: The nvTRPM2 filter is lined by the backbone atoms of Y1035 and G1036, and the side chain of E1037 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: E1037 in nvTRPM2 is replaced by a glutamine in hTRPM2, hTRPM4, and hTRPM5.
source: E1037 in nvTRPM2 is replaced by a glutamine in hTRPM2, hTRPM4, and hTRPM5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, green box).
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequence alignment.

claim: The sequence difference at position 1037 might underlie the much larger Ca2+ preference of the nvTRPM2 pore.
source: This sequence difference might underlie the much larger Ca2+ preference of the nvTRPM2 pore.
evidence: This is a hypothesis connecting sequence differences to functional differences.

claim: The relative permeability for Ca2+ versus Na+ (pCa/pNa) is ~35 for nvTRPM2.
source: Indeed, the relative permeability for Ca2+ versus Na+ (pCa/pNa), estimated from the reversal potential of unitary currents under biionic conditions, is ~35 for nvTRPM2 (Figure 3G, black), as opposed to ~0.45 for hTRPM2 (Figure 3G, blue, replotted from [Tóth and Csanády, 2012]), and ~0 for hTRPM4 (Launay et al., 2002) and hTRPM5 (Liu and Liman, 2003).
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The relative permeability for Ca2+ versus Na+ (pCa/pNa) is ~0.45 for hTRPM2.
source: Indeed, the relative permeability for Ca2+ versus Na+ (pCa/pNa), estimated from the reversal potential of unitary currents under biionic conditions, is ~35 for nvTRPM2 (Figure 3G, black), as opposed to ~0.45 for hTRPM2 (Figure 3G, blue, replotted from [Tóth and Csanády, 2012]), and ~0 for hTRPM4 (Launay et al., 2002) and hTRPM5 (Liu and Liman, 2003).
evidence: This is data replotted from Tóth and Csanády, 2012.

claim: The relative permeability for Ca2+ versus Na+ (pCa/pNa) is ~0 for hTRPM4.
source: Indeed, the relative permeability for Ca2+ versus Na+ (pCa/pNa), estimated from the reversal potential of unitary currents under biionic conditions, is ~35 for nvTRPM2 (Figure 3G, black), as opposed to ~0.45 for hTRPM2 (Figure 3G, blue, replotted from [Tóth and Csanády, 2012]), and ~0 for hTRPM4 (Launay et al., 2002) and hTRPM5 (Liu and Liman, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Launay et al., 2002.

claim: The relative permeability for Ca2+ versus Na+ (pCa/pNa) is ~0 for hTRPM5.
source: Indeed, the relative permeability for Ca2+ versus Na+ (pCa/pNa), estimated from the reversal potential of unitary currents under biionic conditions, is ~35 for nvTRPM2 (Figure 3G, black), as opposed to ~0.45 for hTRPM2 (Figure 3G, blue, replotted from [Tóth and Csanády, 2012]), and ~0 for hTRPM4 (Launay et al., 2002) and hTRPM5 (Liu and Liman, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu and Liman, 2003.

claim: The external vestibule of nvTRPM2 is lined by a double ring of negative charges.
source: The external vestibule of nvTRPM2 is lined by a double ring of negative charges (Figure 3D), the side chains of D1041 and E1042 of the post-filter helix (LDE motif, Figure 3H, inset, red box), and additional negatively charged side chains (E1046 and E1050) line the upper parts of the vestibule (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: The external vestibule of nvTRPM2 is substantially narrower (diameter 10.0 Å) than that of TRPM4 (16.6 Å).
source: It is also substantially narrower (diameter 10.0 Å) than that of TRPM4 (16.6 Å, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C), because the shorter outer pore loop of nvTRPM2 (residues 1045–1055) flips towards the pore (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B), stabilized by a salt bridge between K1047 and E1042 (Figure 3A, blue side chains).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the structure.

claim: The shorter outer pore loop of nvTRPM2 (residues 1045–1055) flips towards the pore, stabilized by a salt bridge between K1047 and E1042.
source: It is also substantially narrower (diameter 10.0 Å) than that of TRPM4 (16.6 Å, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C), because the shorter outer pore loop of nvTRPM2 (residues 1045–1055) flips towards the pore (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B), stabilized by a salt bridge between K1047 and E1042 (Figure 3A, blue side chains).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: Crowding of four times four acidic residues in the tight external vestibule results in a larger negative surface charge density in nvTRPM2 compared to TRPM4.
source: Crowding of four times four acidic residues in the tight external vestibule results in a larger negative surface charge density in nvTRPM2 compared to TRPM4 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and electrostatic calculations.

claim: The nvTRPM2 internal vestibule is tighter (diameter 4.7 Å) than that of TRPM4 (8.5–13 Å).
source: The shape and surface electrostatics of the internal vestibule of TRPM family channels is also diverse (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,D): the nvTRPM2 internal vestibule is tighter (diameter 4.7 Å) than that of TRPM4 (8.5–13 Å), and also much more negative, due to the presence of N1086 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), E1090 (Figure 3A,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and E1094 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the structure.

claim: The nvTRPM2 internal vestibule is much more negative than that of TRPM4, due to the presence of N1086, E1090, and E1094.
source: The shape and surface electrostatics of the internal vestibule of TRPM family channels is also diverse (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,D): the nvTRPM2 internal vestibule is tighter (diameter 4.7 Å) than that of TRPM4 (8.5–13 Å), and also much more negative, due to the presence of N1086 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), E1090 (Figure 3A,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), and E1094 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and electrostatic calculations.

claim: The larger pore diameter and the larger negative surface charge density in both vestibules of nvTRPM2 likely account for its larger throughput rate for cations.
source: The larger pore diameter and the larger negative surface charge density in both vestibules of nvTRPM2 likely account for its larger throughput rate for cations: in symmetrical 144 mM Na+, at negative voltages, unitary conductance approaches ~ 150 pS for nvTRPM2 (Figure 3F, black; note block of outward currents by internal 125 μM Ca2+), as compared to ~25 pS for TRPM4 (Launay et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural features to functional properties.

claim: In symmetrical 144 mM Na+, at negative voltages, unitary conductance approaches ~150 pS for nvTRPM2.
source: The larger pore diameter and the larger negative surface charge density in both vestibules of nvTRPM2 likely account for its larger throughput rate for cations: in symmetrical 144 mM Na+, at negative voltages, unitary conductance approaches ~ 150 pS for nvTRPM2 (Figure 3F, black; note block of outward currents by internal 125 μM Ca2+), as compared to ~25 pS for TRPM4 (Launay et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In symmetrical 144 mM Na+, unitary conductance is ~25 pS for TRPM4.
source: The larger pore diameter and the larger negative surface charge density in both vestibules of nvTRPM2 likely account for its larger throughput rate for cations: in symmetrical 144 mM Na+, at negative voltages, unitary conductance approaches ~ 150 pS for nvTRPM2 (Figure 3F, black; note block of outward currents by internal 125 μM Ca2+), as compared to ~25 pS for TRPM4 (Launay et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Launay et al., 2002.

claim: Human TRPM2 has a large pore diameter.
source: Human TRPM2 also has a large pore diameter (Tóth and Csanády, 2012), but lacks the two acidic residues in the post-filter helix (Figure 3H, inset, red box), and one acidic residue in the internal vestibule.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tóth and Csanády, 2012.

claim: Human TRPM2 lacks the two acidic residues in the post-filter helix and one acidic residue in the internal vestibule.
source: Human TRPM2 also has a large pore diameter (Tóth and Csanády, 2012), but lacks the two acidic residues in the post-filter helix (Figure 3H, inset, red box), and one acidic residue in the internal vestibule.
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequence comparison.

claim: The differences in acidic residues likely account for the intermediate conductance of hTRPM2 (~50 pS in symmetrical 144 mM Na+) between TRPM4 and nvTRPM2.
source: These differences likely account for its intermediate conductance (~50 pS in symmetrical 144 mM Na+, Figure 3F, blue) between TRPM4 and nvTRPM2.
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural differences to functional properties.

claim: Inserting one or two negative charges into the external vestibule of hTRPM2 increased its conductance to ~72 pS, without much effecting relative Ca2+ permeability.
source: Indeed, inserting one or two negative charges into the external vestibule of hTRPM2 increased its conductance to ~72 pS, without much effecting relative Ca2+ permeability (Tóth and Csanády, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tóth and Csanády, 2012.

claim: Inward unitary current of nvTRPM2 in the presence of 12 mM external Ca2+ as the only permeating cation approached −10 pA at negative voltages.
source: Of note, inward unitary current of nvTRPM2 in the presence of 12 mM external Ca2+ as the only permeating cation approached −10 pA at negative voltages (Figure 3G, black symbols), which exceeds the throughput rate expected for a diffusion-limited channel (Hille, 1992).
evidence: This is a measurement from experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The inward unitary current of nvTRPM2 in 12 mM external Ca2+ exceeds the throughput rate expected for a diffusion-limited channel.
source: Of note, inward unitary current of nvTRPM2 in the presence of 12 mM external Ca2+ as the only permeating cation approached −10 pA at negative voltages (Figure 3G, black symbols), which exceeds the throughput rate expected for a diffusion-limited channel (Hille, 1992).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to theoretical expectations from Hille, 1992.

claim: Due to its negative surface, the local concentration of Ca2+ ions in the outer vestibule of nvTRPM2 is far higher than that in the bulk solution.
source: This is a clear indication that, due to its negative surface, the local concentration of Ca2+ ions in the outer vestibule is far higher than that in the bulk solution.
evidence: This is inferred from the high throughput rate exceeding diffusion limits.

claim: An outermost filter binding site formed by a ring of four carboxylates, and additional negative 'recruitment sites' in the outer vestibule, are present in the highly Ca2+-selective TRPV6 channel.
source: Interestingly, an outermost filter binding site formed by a ring of four carboxylates, and additional negative 'recruitment sites' in the outer vestibule, are also present in the highly Ca2+-selective TRPV6 channel (Saotome et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Saotome et al., 2016.

claim: Loss of the LDE motif was suggested to be responsible for the fast inactivation of hTRPM2.
source: Loss of the LDE motif was suggested to be responsible for the fast inactivation of hTRPM2 (Figure 3H, top, left), because its reintroduction abolished rundown (Figure 3H, bottom left, [Tóth and Csanády, 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tóth and Csanády, 2012.

claim: Reintroduction of the LDE motif into hTRPM2 abolished rundown.
source: Loss of the LDE motif was suggested to be responsible for the fast inactivation of hTRPM2 (Figure 3H, top, left), because its reintroduction abolished rundown (Figure 3H, bottom left, [Tóth and Csanády, 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tóth and Csanády, 2012 and shown in Figure 3H.

claim: nvTRPM2, which contains the LDE motif, does not inactivate over the time course of an hour.
source: Consistent with that interpretation, nvTRPM2, which contains this motif, does not inactivate over the time course of an hour (Figure 3H, top, right), but replacing the native LDE triplet with a 'human-like' GY doublet results in clear rundown (time constant 2–3 min; Figure 3H, bottom, right).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Replacing the native LDE triplet in nvTRPM2 with a 'human-like' GY doublet results in clear rundown (time constant 2–3 min).
source: Consistent with that interpretation, nvTRPM2, which contains this motif, does not inactivate over the time course of an hour (Figure 3H, top, right), but replacing the native LDE triplet with a 'human-like' GY doublet results in clear rundown (time constant 2–3 min; Figure 3H, bottom, right).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The presence and proper positioning of D1041 and E1042 seems important for stabilization of the nvTRPM2 pore.
source: Thus, the presence and proper positioning of D1041 and E1042 seems important for stabilization of the nvTRPM2 pore, but the E1042-K1047 salt bridge is not essential, because its disruption by mutations K1047A or K1047E does not result in rundown (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations with mutations.

claim: The E1042-K1047 salt bridge is not essential for preventing rundown, because its disruption by mutations K1047A or K1047E does not result in rundown.
source: Thus, the presence and proper positioning of D1041 and E1042 seems important for stabilization of the nvTRPM2 pore, but the E1042-K1047 salt bridge is not essential, because its disruption by mutations K1047A or K1047E does not result in rundown (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inactivation may be prevented by charge repulsion between the LDE motifs.
source: Possibly, inactivation is prevented by charge repulsion between the LDE motifs, as suggested (Tóth and Csanády, 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Tóth and Csanády, 2012.

claim: The gate of nvTRPM2 is formed by the S6 bundle crossing which constricts the pore to a diameter of less than 2 Å between residues I1082 and N1086.
source: As observed in other TRPM family channels, the gate of nvTRPM2 is formed by the S6 bundle crossing which constricts the pore to a diameter of less than 2 Å between residues I1082 and N1086 (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: The diameter of less than 2 Å at the S6 bundle crossing is too small to allow passage of a water molecule.
source: Because that diameter is too small to allow passage of a water molecule, the observed nvTRPM2 conformation must correspond to a closed gate, as expected in the absence of ADPR.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural measurement and knowledge of water molecule size.

claim: The observed nvTRPM2 conformation corresponds to a closed gate.
source: Because that diameter is too small to allow passage of a water molecule, the observed nvTRPM2 conformation must correspond to a closed gate, as expected in the absence of ADPR.
evidence: This is inferred from the pore diameter and the absence of ADPR in the structure.

claim: S6 of nvTRPM2 shows an α- to π-helix transition in the middle (residues 1073–1077).
source: Additionally, S6 shows an α- to π-helix transition in the middle (residues 1073–1077).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: In TRPV6, S6 is α-helical in the closed state, but in the open state the short π helical break induces a kink and a rotation of the S6 inner segment around a 'gating hinge' alanine (A566), which opens the inner gate.
source: In TRPV6, for which both open- and closed-state structures have been solved (McGoldrick et al., 2018), S6 is α-helical in the closed state, but in the open state the short π helical break induces a kink and a rotation of the S6 inner segment around a 'gating hinge' alanine (A566), which opens the inner gate.
evidence: This is supported by citation to McGoldrick et al., 2018.

claim: The π-helical break in S6 is a common feature seen in most reported TRP channel structures, except for TRPV2 and TRPV6 in the closed state.
source: Interestingly, the π-helical break in S6 is a common feature seen in most reported TRP channel structures, except for TRPV2 and TRPV6 in the closed state (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), and even the gating-hinge alanine is conserved in some TRPM family members such as TRPM1, TRPM3, and TRPM4 (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparative observation across multiple TRP channel structures.

claim: The gating-hinge alanine is conserved in some TRPM family members such as TRPM1, TRPM3, and TRPM4.
source: Interestingly, the π-helical break in S6 is a common feature seen in most reported TRP channel structures, except for TRPV2 and TRPV6 in the closed state (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), and even the gating-hinge alanine is conserved in some TRPM family members such as TRPM1, TRPM3, and TRPM4 (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2017.

claim: Although the solved structures of TRPM4 are closed, the corresponding region of S6 is π-helical.
source: However, although the solved structures of TRPM4 are closed, the corresponding region of S6 is π-helical (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from TRPM4 structures.

claim: Gate opening in TRPM channels is probably not triggered by the α- to π-helix transition of S6.
source: Thus, unlike for TRPV6, gate opening in TRPM channels is probably not triggered by the α- to π-helix transition of S6 (McGoldrick et al., 2018), but likely resembles opening of TRPV1, in which the S6 bundle crossing opens via direct expansion (Cao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with TRPV6 and TRPV1 gating mechanisms.

claim: Gate opening in TRPM channels likely resembles opening of TRPV1, in which the S6 bundle crossing opens via direct expansion.
source: Thus, unlike for TRPV6, gate opening in TRPM channels is probably not triggered by the α- to π-helix transition of S6 (McGoldrick et al., 2018), but likely resembles opening of TRPV1, in which the S6 bundle crossing opens via direct expansion (Cao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with TRPV1 gating mechanism and supported by citation to Cao et al., 2013.

claim: Clear density for a bound Ca2+ ion is seen, occluded into each subunit of nvTRPM2.
source: Although the nvTRPM2 structure was obtained in the presence of trace amounts of Ca2+ (free Ca2+ concentration in an unbuffered saline with no added Ca2+ is in the micromolar range, for example, [Csanády and Adam-Vizi, 2003]), clear density for a bound Ca2+ ion is seen, occluded into each subunit.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM map.

claim: The Ca2+ binding site is formed by the cytosolic ends of transmembrane helices S2 and S3, and the S2-S3 linker helix.
source: The Ca2+ binding site, formed by the cytosolic ends of transmembrane helices S2 and S3, and the S2-S3 linker helix, is located at the membrane-cytosol interface (Figure 4A–C), and is accessible from the protein surface through a narrow opening ('peripheral tunnel'; Figure 4A, arrow).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: The Ca2+ binding site is located at the membrane-cytosol interface.
source: The Ca2+ binding site, formed by the cytosolic ends of transmembrane helices S2 and S3, and the S2-S3 linker helix, is located at the membrane-cytosol interface (Figure 4A–C), and is accessible from the protein surface through a narrow opening ('peripheral tunnel'; Figure 4A, arrow).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: The Ca2+ binding site is accessible from the protein surface through a narrow opening ('peripheral tunnel').
source: The Ca2+ binding site, formed by the cytosolic ends of transmembrane helices S2 and S3, and the S2-S3 linker helix, is located at the membrane-cytosol interface (Figure 4A–C), and is accessible from the protein surface through a narrow opening ('peripheral tunnel'; Figure 4A, arrow).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: The bound Ca2+ ion is coordinated by the side chains of residues E893 and Q896 of S2 and N918 and D921 of S3 in a pentacovalent geometry.
source: The bound Ca2+ ion is coordinated by the side chains of residues E893 and Q896 of S2 and N918 and D921 of S3 in a pentacovalent geometry, E893 provides two coordinate bonds to the ion (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: E893 provides two coordinate bonds to the Ca2+ ion.
source: The bound Ca2+ ion is coordinated by the side chains of residues E893 and Q896 of S2 and N918 and D921 of S3 in a pentacovalent geometry, E893 provides two coordinate bonds to the ion (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: The side chain of E1110 lines the bottom wall of the peripheral tunnel.
source: TRP helix one is located right below the Ca2+ site, and the side chain of E1110 (Figure 4C) lines the bottom wall of the peripheral tunnel (Figure 4B), facilitating access of the cation to its binding site.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: E1110 forms a hydrogen bond with the side chain of Q896, keeping the latter properly oriented for Ca2+ coordination.
source: It also forms a hydrogen bond with the side chain of Q896, keeping the latter properly oriented for Ca2+ coordination.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: The five residues involved in Ca2+ coordination (E893, Q896, N918, D921, E1110) are conserved between TRPM2, 4, 5 and 8.
source: These five residues are conserved between TRPM2, 4, 5 and 8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, orange boxes), and the geometry of Ca2+ coordination in nvTRPM2 resembles that seen in the Ca2+ bound structure of hTRPM4 (Autzen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequence alignment.

claim: The geometry of Ca2+ coordination in nvTRPM2 resembles that seen in the Ca2+ bound structure of hTRPM4.
source: These five residues are conserved between TRPM2, 4, 5 and 8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, orange boxes), and the geometry of Ca2+ coordination in nvTRPM2 resembles that seen in the Ca2+ bound structure of hTRPM4 (Autzen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Autzen et al., 2018.

claim: Macroscopic nvTRPM2 channel currents show a somewhat higher apparent affinity for activation by cytosolic Ca2+ compared to hTRPM2.
source: Compared to hTRPM2, macroscopic nvTRPM2 channel currents show a somewhat higher apparent affinity for activation by cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 4D, left); a reduction of inward macroscopic current by millimolar cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 4D, right) reflects a reduction in unitary current amplitude due to pore block (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A reduction of inward macroscopic current by millimolar cytosolic Ca2+ reflects a reduction in unitary current amplitude due to pore block.
source: Compared to hTRPM2, macroscopic nvTRPM2 channel currents show a somewhat higher apparent affinity for activation by cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 4D, left); a reduction of inward macroscopic current by millimolar cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 4D, right) reflects a reduction in unitary current amplitude due to pore block (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of macroscopic and unitary currents shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: The Ca2+ dependence of nvTRPM2 channel open probability is characterized by a K1/2 of ~2 μM.
source: Correcting for the latter effect reveals the Ca2+ dependence of channel open probability (Figure 4F), characterized by a K1/2 of ~2 μM (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The Q896A, N918A, and D921A nvTRPM2 mutants generated functional channels.
source: The Q896A, N918A, and D921A nvTRPM2 mutants generated functional channels, but in each case current activation required larger free cytosolic Ca2+ concentrations (Figure 4G–I; Figure 4K, left), reporting a dramatic loss of Ca2+ sensitivity.
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figures 4G-I.

claim: Current activation of Q896A, N918A, and D921A nvTRPM2 mutants required larger free cytosolic Ca2+ concentrations, reporting a dramatic loss of Ca2+ sensitivity.
source: The Q896A, N918A, and D921A nvTRPM2 mutants generated functional channels, but in each case current activation required larger free cytosolic Ca2+ concentrations (Figure 4G–I; Figure 4K, left), reporting a dramatic loss of Ca2+ sensitivity.
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figures 4G-I and 4K.

claim: Estimated K1/2 for channel activation was ~40 μM for Q896A nvTRPM2.
source: Estimated K1/2 for channel activation was ~40 μM for Q896A, whereas for N918A and D921A open probability failed to saturate even at 1250 μM (K1/2 >1 mM).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data.

claim: For N918A and D921A nvTRPM2 mutants, open probability failed to saturate even at 1250 μM Ca2+ (K1/2 >1 mM).
source: Estimated K1/2 for channel activation was ~40 μM for Q896A, whereas for N918A and D921A open probability failed to saturate even at 1250 μM (K1/2 >1 mM).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data.

claim: The E1110A mutant displayed a more modest reduction in apparent Ca2+ affinity (K1/2 ~12 μM).
source: The E1110A mutant displayed a more modest reduction in apparent Ca2+ affinity (Figure 4J, Figure 4K, green bars; K1/2 ~12 μM), consistent with the less direct involvement of the E1110 side chain in Ca2+ binding (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data shown in Figures 4J and 4K.

claim: The more modest reduction in Ca2+ affinity for E1110A is consistent with the less direct involvement of the E1110 side chain in Ca2+ binding.
source: The E1110A mutant displayed a more modest reduction in apparent Ca2+ affinity (Figure 4J, Figure 4K, green bars; K1/2 ~12 μM), consistent with the less direct involvement of the E1110 side chain in Ca2+ binding (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural observations to functional data.

claim: E893A nvTRPM2 channels failed to open even in the presence of millimolar cytosolic Ca2+.
source: In contrast, E893A channels failed to open even in the presence of millimolar cytosolic Ca2+, underscoring the exquisite importance of this residue in Ca2+ coordination (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data.

claim: The Ca2+ binding site mutants were all robustly stimulated by PIP2.
source: Interestingly, the Ca2+ binding site mutants were all robustly stimulated by PIP2: in contrast to wild-type (WT) channel currents that were stimulated only by 10–20% (Figure 1B), the currents for the mutants were enhanced by up to 20-fold upon PIP2 addition (Figure 4G–J; Figure 4K, rightmost bars).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figures 4G-J and 4K.

claim: The currents for the Ca2+ binding site mutants were enhanced by up to 20-fold upon PIP2 addition.
source: Interestingly, the Ca2+ binding site mutants were all robustly stimulated by PIP2: in contrast to wild-type (WT) channel currents that were stimulated only by 10–20% (Figure 1B), the currents for the mutants were enhanced by up to 20-fold upon PIP2 addition (Figure 4G–J; Figure 4K, rightmost bars).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figures 4G-J and 4K.

claim: Suppression of hTRPM2 activity upon PIP2 depletion was shown to be counteracted by raising cytosolic Ca2+.
source: Conversely, suppression of hTRPM2 activity upon PIP2 depletion was shown to be counteracted by raising cytosolic Ca2+ (Tóth and Csanády, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tóth and Csanády, 2012.

claim: When the side chains involved in Ca2+ coordination are intact, Ca2+ binds so tightly that the binding sites are saturated at 125 μM free Ca2+.
source: Clearly, when the side chains involved in its coordination are intact, Ca2+ binds so tightly that the binding sites are saturated at 125 μM free Ca2+: under such conditions channel open probability is close-to-maximal even when the PIP2 sites are not fully occupied, and adding exogenous PIP2 causes little further current enhancement.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations with wild-type and mutant channels.

claim: Density for a phospholipid molecule is seen near the bound Ca2+ ion, in the immediate vicinity of the TRP box region of TRP helix 1.
source: Indeed, density for a phospholipid molecule is seen near the bound Ca2+ ion, in the immediate vicinity of the TRP box region of TRP helix 1 (Figure 4C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM map.

claim: The phospholipid headgroup near the Ca2+ binding site was not clearly resolved.
source: The phospholipid headgroup was not clearly resolved, and the phosphate moiety of the modeled phosphatidic acid is too far (~9 Å) from the cation to be involved in its coordination.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the cryo-EM map.

claim: The terminal phosphates of a PIP2 molecule bound in the same position could potentially contact the bound Ca2+ ion.
source: However, the terminal phosphates of a PIP2 molecule bound in the same position could potentially contact the bound Ca2+ ion.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed phospholipid density.

claim: The upper chamber represents a relatively secluded volume of ~50000 A3, buried inside the protein.
source: The empty upper chamber represents a relatively secluded volume of ~50000 A3, buried inside the protein (Figure 5B, Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct calculation from the structure.

claim: The upper chamber communicates with the cytosol through eight large lateral windows.
source: At its sides, the upper chamber communicates with the cytosol through eight large lateral windows, four between the bottom and middle tier (NTD and LHD) (Figure 2F), and four between the middle and the top tier (LHD and PD) (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: The upper chamber is directly connected to the Ca2+ binding sites through four tunnels ('central tunnels').
source: In addition, the upper chamber is directly connected to the Ca2+ binding sites through four tunnels (Figure 5B, 'central tunnels').
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: The Ca2+ binding site can be viewed as a recess in a bent tunnel with a diameters > 4 Å that connects the upper chamber with the cytosol.
source: Indeed, the Ca2+ binding site can be viewed as a recess in a bent tunnel with a diameters > 4 Å (Figure 5B, inset) that connects the upper chamber with the cytosol (Figure 5C, Video 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the structure.

claim: In nvTRPM2 the surface electrostatics of both the peripheral and the central tunnel is negative.
source: In nvTRPM2 the surface electrostatics of both the peripheral and the central tunnel is negative (Figure 5C, left).
evidence: This is calculated from the structure and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In TRPM2, Ca2+ entering through the open pore can directly access the activating sites, without leaving the protein interior.
source: Thus, in TRPM2, which is highly Ca2+ permeable, Ca2+ entering through the open pore can directly access the activating sites, without leaving the protein interior (Figure 5C, left, yellow arrows).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural features of the tunnels and their electrostatics.

claim: In TRPM4, both the peripheral and central tunnels exist, but their surfaces are positive.
source: Interestingly, although both tunnels exist in TRPM4, their surfaces are positive (Figure 5C, right).
evidence: This is calculated from the TRPM4 structure and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For hTRPM2, the activating Ca2+ sites were shown to be inaccessible to extracellular Ca2+ in the closed-pore state, but saturated by extracellular Ca2+ entering through the pore in the open-channel state.
source: For hTRPM2 the activating Ca2+ sites were shown to be inaccessible to extracellular Ca2+ in the closed-pore state, but saturated by extracellular Ca2+ entering through the pore in the open-channel state, leading to the suggestion that these sites are intracellular, but buried in some deep crevice, shielded from the protein surface, near the intracellular mouth of the pore (Csanády and Töröcsik, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Csanády and Töröcsik, 2009.

claim: The location of the Ca2+ binding sites in nvTRPM2 is consistent with the prediction that they are intracellular, but buried in some deep crevice, shielded from the protein surface, near the intracellular mouth of the pore.
source: The location of the Ca2+ binding sites in nvTRPM2 (Figure 5B–C) is consistent with that prediction.
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural observations to previous functional predictions.

claim: In the absence of extracellular Ca2+, addition and removal of cytosolic Ca2+ caused nvTRPM2 currents to activate and deactivate, respectively, regardless of the applied membrane potential.
source: Indeed, in the absence of extracellular (pipette) Ca2+ (Figure 5D), addition and removal of cytosolic Ca2+ (gray bars) in the continuous presence of ADPR (black bar) caused nvTRPM2 currents to activate and deactivate, respectively, regardless of the applied membrane potential (colored bar and shading); the time constants of current decay in response to cytosolic Ca2+ removal (colored fit lines and numbers (in ms)) attested to a modest intrinsic voltage dependence of gating (Figure 5F, green symbols).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figures 5D and 5F.

claim: When extracellular [Ca2+] was 1 mM, currents evoked by addition of ADPR+Ca2+ could be completely abolished by cytosolic Ca2+ removal only when the membrane potential was positive.
source: However, when extracellular [Ca2+] was 1 mM (Figure 5E), currents evoked by addition of ADPR+Ca2+ (black and gray bars) could be completely abolished by cytosolic Ca2+ removal only when the membrane potential was positive (Figure 5E, gray shading), i.e., when the driving force for Ca2+ influx through the pore was small.
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: At moderately positive voltages (+20 to+40 mV) the decay time constants upon cytosolic Ca2+ removal were greatly prolonged by the presence of external Ca2+.
source: Even at moderately positive voltages (+20 to+40 mV) the decay time constants upon cytosolic Ca2+ removal (red fit lines and numbers (in ms)) were greatly prolonged by the presence of external Ca2+ (Figure 5F, purple symbols), approaching those measured in its absence (Figure 5F, green symbols) only at extremely positive voltages (+60 to +80 mV) at which the driving force for Ca2+ influx is negligible.
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: As long as the gate is open, Ca2+ entering through the nvTRPM2 pore can directly reach the Ca2+ sites through the central tunnels, and keep them saturated even while the protein surface is continuously rinsed with a Ca2+-free solution.
source: Such slowing of channel closure by external Ca2+ has been described for hTRPM2 (Csanády and Töröcsik, 2009), and suggests that, as long as the gate is open, Ca2+ entering through the nvTRPM2 pore can directly reach the Ca2+ sites through the central tunnels, and keep them saturated even while the protein surface is continuously rinsed with a Ca2+-free solution.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and structural features.

claim: At negative membrane potentials that provide a large driving force for the influx of millimolar extracellular Ca2+, a substantial fraction of nvTRPM2 current survived cytosolic Ca2+ removal.
source: By contrast, at negative membrane potentials (Figure 5E, white shading, Figure 6B) that provide a large driving force for the influx of millimolar extracellular Ca2+, a substantial fraction of nvTRPM2 current survived cytosolic Ca2+ removal (Figure 5E, yellow arrows), and subsided only when ADPR was also removed.
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figures 5E and 6B.

claim: At negative voltages, in the presence of external Ca2+, nvTRPM2 currents activate, albeit with a delay, upon addition of cytosolic ADPR even in the absence of cytosolic Ca2+.
source: Fourth, the perhaps most compelling argument against Ca2+ accumulation at the patch surface being responsible for the residual currents in Figure 5E, (yellow arrows) is our finding that at negative voltages, in the presence of external Ca2+, nvTRPM2 currents activate, albeit with a delay, upon addition of cytosolic ADPR even in the absence of cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 6B, right): the magnitude of that 'spontaneous' current is identical to that which survives removal of pre-applied cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 6B, left).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The magnitude of the 'spontaneous' current activated by ADPR alone is identical to that which survives removal of pre-applied cytosolic Ca2+.
source: Fourth, the perhaps most compelling argument against Ca2+ accumulation at the patch surface being responsible for the residual currents in Figure 5E, (yellow arrows) is our finding that at negative voltages, in the presence of external Ca2+, nvTRPM2 currents activate, albeit with a delay, upon addition of cytosolic ADPR even in the absence of cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 6B, right): the magnitude of that 'spontaneous' current is identical to that which survives removal of pre-applied cytosolic Ca2+ (Figure 6B, left).
evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The delayed activation of spontaneous current must reflect a very low 'spontaneous' channel opening rate of ADPR-bound channels in the absence of bound Ca2+.
source: Because the spontaneous current activates from a state in which all pores in the patch have been closed for several seconds (Figure 6A–B, section (e)), a duration more than sufficient to completely wash off even very high concentrations of pre-applied cytosolic Ca2+ (cf., Figure 1A), it cannot be explained by bulk Ca2+ accumulation. Rather, its delayed activation must reflect a very low 'spontaneous' channel opening rate of ADPR-bound channels in the absence of bound Ca2+ (Figure 6A, section (f)): upon the first such spontaneous opening of a channel its upper chamber is immediately flooded by Ca2+ which henceforth maintains that channel in an active state (Figure 6A, section (g)).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Upon the first spontaneous opening of a channel its upper chamber is immediately flooded by Ca2+ which henceforth maintains that channel in an active state.
source: Because the spontaneous current activates from a state in which all pores in the patch have been closed for several seconds (Figure 6A–B, section (e)), a duration more than sufficient to completely wash off even very high concentrations of pre-applied cytosolic Ca2+ (cf., Figure 1A), it cannot be explained by bulk Ca2+ accumulation. Rather, its delayed activation must reflect a very low 'spontaneous' channel opening rate of ADPR-bound channels in the absence of bound Ca2+ (Figure 6A, section (f)): upon the first such spontaneous opening of a channel its upper chamber is immediately flooded by Ca2+ which henceforth maintains that channel in an active state (Figure 6A, section (g)).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and structural features.

claim: The larger pore diameter and larger negative surface charge of both pore vestibules in nvTRPM2 explains its higher Ca2+ permeability and larger conductance compared to TRPM4.
source: In particular, the larger pore diameter and larger negative surface charge of both pore vestibules in nvTRPM2 explains its higher Ca2+ permeability and larger conductance compared to TRPM4.
evidence: This is a summary inference connecting structural features to functional properties.

claim: Loss of the sequence segment corresponding to the external vestibule helix explains inactivation of human TRPM2.
source: The external vestibule of nvTRPM2 is stabilized by a negatively charged short helix. Loss of the corresponding sequence segment explains inactivation of human TRPM2 (Tóth and Csanády, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural differences to functional properties, supported by citation.

claim: Changes in Ca2+- and PIP2-sensitivity upon truncation of Ca2+-coordinating amino acid side chains suggest a mechanism for gating regulation by these two channel cofactors.
source: Changes in Ca2+- and PIP2-sensitivity upon truncation of Ca2+-coordinating amino acid side chains suggest a mechanism for gating regulation by these two channel cofactors.
evidence: This is a summary inference from the mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The secluded location of the activating Ca2+ sites in the protein interior in a recess of a narrow tunnel that connects the upper chamber of the cytoplasmic cavity to the cytosol, and the negative surface charge of this tunnel in TRPM2, explain the unique dependence of TRPM2 activity on intra- and extracellular Ca2+.
source: The secluded location of the activating Ca2+ sites in the protein interior in a recess of a narrow tunnel that connects the upper chamber of the cytoplasmic cavity to the cytosol, and the negative surface charge of this tunnel in TRPM2, explain the unique dependence of TRPM2 activity on intra- and extracellular Ca2+.
evidence: This is a summary inference connecting structural features to functional properties.

claim: Although the Ca2+ sites are intracellular in both TRPM4 and TRPM2, their regulation through Ca2+ is fundamentally different.
source: Thus, although the Ca2+ sites are intracellular in both TRPM4 and TRPM2, their regulation through Ca2+ is fundamentally different.
evidence: This is a summary inference from structural and functional comparisons.

claim: TRPM4 activity requires a continuous supply of cytosolic Ca2+ that enters through its peripheral tunnel.
source: TRPM4 activity requires a continuous supply of cytosolic Ca2+ that enters through its peripheral tunnel.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural features and functional properties of TRPM4.

claim: ADPR-bound TRPM2 requires only an initiator Ca2+ spark from the cytosol, to then remain activated by Ca2+ ions that enter through its pore and access the binding site through the central tunnel.
source: In contrast, ADPR-bound TRPM2 requires only an initiator Ca2+ spark from the cytosol (Figure 6A, section (b)), to then remain activated by Ca2+ ions that enter through its pore and access the binding site through the central tunnel (Figure 6A, section (c)).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and structural features.

claim: Extremely Ca2+ permeable nvTRPM2 does not even require an initiator spark: infrequent spontaneous openings of ADPR-bound channels allow for self-activation using exclusively extracellular Ca2+.
source: Indeed, extremely Ca2+ permeable nvTRPM2 does not even require an initiator spark: infrequent spontaneous openings of ADPR-bound channels allow for self-activation using exclusively extracellular Ca2+ (Figure 6A, sections (f-g)) – that mechanism might be relevant even for moderately Ca2+ permeable hTRPM2 under the static conditions of a living cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: The self-activation mechanism using exclusively extracellular Ca2+ might be relevant even for moderately Ca2+ permeable hTRPM2 under the static conditions of a living cell.
source: Indeed, extremely Ca2+ permeable nvTRPM2 does not even require an initiator spark: infrequent spontaneous openings of ADPR-bound channels allow for self-activation using exclusively extracellular Ca2+ (Figure 6A, sections (f-g)) – that mechanism might be relevant even for moderately Ca2+ permeable hTRPM2 under the static conditions of a living cell.
evidence: This is a speculation about the physiological relevance of the observed mechanism.

claim: TRPM2 plays key roles in migration and chemokine production of immune cells.
source: TRPM2 plays key roles in migration and chemokine production of immune cells (Yamamoto et al., 2008; Knowles et al., 2011), insulin secretion (Uchida et al., 2011), and body heat control (Song et al., 2016; Tan and McNaughton, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yamamoto et al., 2008 and Knowles et al., 2011.

source: Under pathological conditions such as stroke and myocardial infarction TRPM2 activity leads to apoptosis (Nilius et al., 2007), and genetic linkage studies strongly suggest its involvement in the development of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Parkinsonism Dementia (Hermosura et al., 2008), and bipolar disorder (McQuillin et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nilius et al., 2007.

claim: Genetic linkage studies strongly suggest TRPM2 involvement in the development of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Parkinsonism Dementia.
source: Under pathological conditions such as stroke and myocardial infarction TRPM2 activity leads to apoptosis (Nilius et al., 2007), and genetic linkage studies strongly suggest its involvement in the development of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Parkinsonism Dementia (Hermosura et al., 2008), and bipolar disorder (McQuillin et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hermosura et al., 2008.

claim: Genetic linkage studies strongly suggest TRPM2 involvement in the development of bipolar disorder.
source: Under pathological conditions such as stroke and myocardial infarction TRPM2 activity leads to apoptosis (Nilius et al., 2007), and genetic linkage studies strongly suggest its involvement in the development of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Parkinsonism Dementia (Hermosura et al., 2008), and bipolar disorder (McQuillin et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McQuillin et al., 2006 and Xu et al., 2006.

claim: TRPM2 is an emerging therapeutic target for chronic inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases, diabetes, and hyperinsulinism.
source: TRPM2 is therefore an emerging therapeutic target for chronic inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases, diabetes, and hyperinsulinism.
evidence: This is inferred from the pathological roles of TRPM2.

claim: TRPM2 is a Ca2+ permeable non-selective cation channel opened by simultaneous binding of three obligate co-activators, cytosolic ADP-ribose (ADPR), Ca2+, and membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2).
source: TRPM2 is a Ca2+ permeable non-selective cation channel opened by simultaneous binding of three obligate co-activators, cytosolic ADP-ribose (ADPR) (Perraud et al., 2001; Sano et al., 2001; Hara et al., 2002), Ca2+ (Csanády and Töröcsik, 2009), and membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) (Tóth and Csanády, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: TRPM2 is activated by cytosolic ADP-ribose (ADPR).
source: TRPM2 is a Ca2+ permeable non-selective cation channel opened by simultaneous binding of three obligate co-activators, cytosolic ADP-ribose (ADPR) (Perraud et al., 2001; Sano et al., 2001; Hara et al., 2002), Ca2+ (Csanády and Töröcsik, 2009), and membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) (Tóth and Csanády, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Perraud et al., 2001; Sano et al., 2001; Hara et al., 2002.

claim: TRPM2 is activated by cytosolic Ca2+.

claim: TRPM2 is activated by membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2).

claim: Regulation by Ca2+ and PIP2 are interrelated through a mechanism which is not understood.

claim: In TRPM2 a C-terminal ~270 residue NUDT9-homology (NUDT9H) domain serves to bind ADPR.
source: In TRPM2 a C-terminal ~270 residue NUDT9-homology (NUDT9H) domain serves to bind ADPR (Perraud et al., 2001).

claim: TRPM2 and TRPM4 are both activated by cytosolic Ca2+.
source: TRPM2 and TRPM4 are both activated by cytosolic Ca2+.

claim: TRPM4 is monovalent selective.
source: However, as TRPM4 is monovalent selective, its activation requires a nearby Ca2+ source, such as a co-localized Ca2+ channel (Launay et al., 2002; Kraft and Harteneck, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Launay et al., 2002 and Kraft and Harteneck, 2005.

claim: TRPM4 activation requires a nearby Ca2+ source, such as a co-localized Ca2+ channel.

claim: TRPM2 is itself Ca2+ permeable, which provides a unique mechanism for positive feedback.
